original.title: Ἀγαθὰ καὶ κακά.
paragraphs: Ὑπὸ τῶν κακῶν τὰ ἀγαθὰ ἐδιώχθη ὡς ἀσθενῆ ὅντα:
εἰς οὐρανὸν δὲ ἀνῆλθεν.
Τὰ δὲ ἀγαθὰ ἠρώτησαν τὸν Δία πῶς εἶναι μετ'ἀνθρώπων.
Ὁ δὲ εἶπεν <μὴ> μετ' ἀλλήλων πάντα,
ἓν δὲ καθ' ἓν τοῖς ἀνθρώποις ἐπέρχεσθαι.
Διὰ τοῦτο τὰ μὲν κακὰ συνεχῆ τοῖς ἀνθρώποις,
ὡς πλησίον ὄντα, ἐπέρχεται,
τὰ δὲ ἀγαθὰ βράδιον,
ἐξ οὐρανοῦ κατιόντα.
Ὅτι ἀγαθῶν μὲν οὐδεὶς ταχέως ἐπιτυγχάνει,
ὑπὸ δὲ τῶν κακῶν ἕκαστος καθ' ἑκάστην πλήττεται.

translation.title: Blessings and Misfortunes
paragraphs: Blessings were driven away by Misfortunes on the grounds that they were weak;
they ascended to heaven.
The Blessings asked Zeus how they might exist among humans.
He replied that they should not all go together,
but rather that each should come to humans one by one.
For this reason, Misfortunes befall humans continuously,
being close by,
whereas good things arrive more slowly,
descending from heaven.
This illustrates that no one attains good things quickly,
while everyone is struck by bad things at every turn.

transliteration.title: The Blessings and the Misfortunes
paragraphs: The Misfortunes once expelled the Blessings because [they] were weak;
[they] raised to heaven.
The blessings asked Manwë how ‹they will exist› may among Men.
He replied ‹to them› that not together ‹they will go› should,
but rather that each ‹will come› to Men ‹each individually›.
For reason this, misfortunes happen ever against men,
being ‹close by›
while blessings come ‹more slow›,
descending from heaven.
This illuminates that ‹no one› obtains blessings fast,
while everyone [is] shot by misfortunes ‹many times›.

roman.title: In·eliaid ah in·egmoer
paragraphs: In·egmoer erlu ennistanner in·eliaid añ gaeth i nîr wisg;
erianner na venel.
In·eliaid mabenner Manwe movan dhathar ce mig Edain.
Te dambent andin i ú vinegel menathar aen,
ach hennui i elia tolatha n'Edain erelia.
Añ gaeth hen, egmoer hídar ui dan Edain,
noed edos,
lo eliaid telir eñgwir,
duiad o venel.
Se celia i alphen gêd eliaid lim,
lo ilphen píthannen vo egmoer laelo.
